title: How do you give your agent a key without giving it your password?
checkedAgainst: the Personal Agent Protocol draft 1.0 (in progress; as published on 2026-11-13), read and not run: `model.test.ts` holds the model to the rules and examples of its sections 4.1 to 4.7, 5.4, 5.5, 10.5 and 10.8, including 1.0's prompt=consent, consent page and Pushed Authorization Requests, each test naming its section, and checks the draft's PKCE challenge against RFC 7636's verifier with real SHA-256, using the RFC's Appendix B values in `fixtures/rfc7636-appendix-b.json`. There is no reference implementation here to run the model against. It is also held to what the protocol itself publishes, copied on 2026-11-13 into `fixtures/poppy-official.json`: the client metadata, device authorization response and auth pass the Company kit's JSON Schemas, and they and the issuer metadata give the values of spec.md's examples.

answer: Your password stays on the Company's own page; the agent gets a key cut to what you approved, revocable on its own

questions.question: The agent asks for orders:read and orders:write, and you approve only orders:read. What does the token response say, and how does the agent get orders:write for the exchange?
questions.answer: The response’s scope says orders:read, so the agent sees orders:write is missing. You sign in again and it asks for orders:read orders:write, everything it still needs; the new refresh token pat_3Fz9 replaces pat_8Hk2.

questions.question: During Direct Sign-In, a response from shoes.example's sign-in, with a code in it, reaches the agent's redirect. What stops it?
questions.answer: The agent rejects it: its iss names https://auth.shoes.example, and the agent started sign-in with https://auth.example.com.

questions.question: During Device Sign-In, the link the agent is given to show you is https://auth.shoes.example/device. What does the agent do?
questions.answer: It does not show the link: its host auth.shoes.example is neither auth.example.com nor example.com, nor a subdomain of either. A link it shows has Example Company and example.com beside it.

questions.question: A thief copies the agent's refresh token and sends it to the token endpoint with a client assertion of its own. What comes back?
questions.answer: invalid_grant: the refresh token was issued to https://agent.example/agent.json. The thief can sign an assertion only as itself.

questions.question: Suppose your agent signed in by typing your password into the website instead. What can the Company do if the agent misbehaves?
questions.answer: It sees you, not agent.example, so it can limit nothing and can only block it entirely. Through sign-in it could revoke agent.example’s refresh tokens without affecting you.

steps.title: The shortcut: hand over your password
steps.line: Predict: what can the Company do if it misbehaves?
steps.caption: You want your agent to exchange a jacket at example.com, and that needs your account. The quick way is to give the agent your password and let it sign in on the website as you. Then the Company sees you, not an agent. It cannot limit what the agent does, and if the agent misbehaves, it can only block it entirely. Poppy’s sign-in is there so the agent does not need your password.
steps.picture: The shortcut. Your agent holds your password and types it into example.com’s own sign-in page. The Company sees you, not an agent: it cannot limit what the agent does, and can only stop it by blocking it entirely. The rule, from section 10.5 of the draft: an agent that signs in with your credentials looks like you.

steps.title: The agent opens the Company’s own page
steps.line: It asks for two scopes, and nothing more.
steps.caption: Poppy’s way is OAuth. The agent opens example.com’s sign-in page in your browser and asks for the two scopes the exchange needs, orders:read and orders:write, and not addresses. The Company describes each scope and warns that orders:write can’t be undone. The request carries a fingerprint of the agent’s secret PKCE verifier, so only the agent can finish this sign-in, and prompt=consent, so the page appears even for scopes you approved before: a forwarded link cannot get tokens without it.
steps.picture: The Company’s page in your browser, open at auth.example.com asks you to sign in and approve orders:read and orders:write; your password is still with you. The agent holds no key and no refresh token. The agent opened the Company’s authorization page in your browser, asking for orders:read and orders:write, with a PKCE challenge and prompt=consent. The Session Yx2b7Q and User ID usr_Q7c1vK are untouched by sign-in. The rule, from section 4.2 of the draft: The agent opens the Company’s own page in your browser, asking only for the scopes the task needs.

steps.title: You sign in there, and approve less
steps.line: Your password goes to the Company, and no further.
steps.caption: You sign in on the Company’s page, with your password or however example.com allows. You tick orders:read, to look first, and leave orders:write. You may approve fewer scopes than the agent asked for. That is the whole idea: Your password stays on the Company's own page; the agent gets a key cut to what you approved, revocable on its own.
steps.picture: The Company’s page in your browser, open at auth.example.com holds your password, and you approved orders:read and left orders:write unticked. The agent holds no key and no refresh token. You signed in on the Company’s page and approved orders:read. The Session Yx2b7Q and User ID usr_Q7c1vK are untouched by sign-in. The rule, from section 4.7 of the draft: You may approve fewer scopes than asked, and the Company grants none beyond those asked.

steps.title: A code from another Company is refused
steps.line: Its iss names shoes.example, so the agent drops it.
steps.caption: Before your answer comes back, a response arrives at the agent’s address from another Company’s sign-in, with a code in it. Each response names the Company that sent it, in a field called iss, and the agent compares it with the Company it started with: auth.shoes.example is not auth.example.com. The agent rejects it, and what it holds does not change. That keeps another sign-in from being swapped in.

last.reason: its iss names https://auth.shoes.example, and the agent started sign-in with https://auth.example.com

after.reason: its iss names https://auth.shoes.example, and the agent started sign-in with https://auth.example.com

steps.picture: The Company’s page in your browser, open at auth.example.com holds your password, and you approved orders:read and left orders:write unticked. The agent holds no key and no refresh token. A response from shoes.example’s sign-in reached the agent’s redirect and rejected it: its iss names https://auth.shoes.example, and the agent started sign-in with https://auth.example.com. The Session Yx2b7Q and User ID usr_Q7c1vK are untouched by sign-in. The rule, from section 4.2 of the draft: The agent checks that iss names the Company it started sign-in with.

steps.title: A one-time code only the agent can redeem
steps.line: The key comes back with one tooth: orders:read.
steps.caption: Your browser returns to the agent’s own address with a one-time code. The Company sends codes to an address the agent registered, matched exactly, and to nowhere else. The agent takes the code to the Company with its signed client assertion and its PKCE verifier, which must match the fingerprint. Back comes a key cut with one tooth, for orders:read, and a tag that brings new keys.

before.reason: its iss names https://auth.shoes.example, and the agent started sign-in with https://auth.example.com

steps.picture: No sign-in page is open in your browser. The agent holds a key with one tooth, for orders:read, and the refresh token pat_8Hk2. Your browser brought a one-time code to the agent’s registered redirect; the agent checked iss and redeemed the code with its client assertion and PKCE verifier, and the token endpoint returned a key cut for orders:read, its scope saying so. The Session Yx2b7Q and User ID usr_Q7c1vK are untouched by sign-in. The rule, from section 4.2 of the draft: The code comes back only to a registered redirect, and only the agent can redeem it.

steps.title: To do more, ask for everything again
steps.line: Both scopes asked again; the old tag still works.
steps.caption: The response said orders:read, so the exchange is out of reach. The agent asks you again, and asks for orders:read and orders:write, everything it still needs, not just the missing scope. This time you approve both. Until the new sign-in finishes, the agent keeps the key and tag it has: a sign-in that is pending, or fails, changes nothing it holds.
steps.picture: The Company’s page in your browser, open at auth.example.com holds your password, and you approved orders:read orders:write. The agent holds a key with one tooth, for orders:read, and the refresh token pat_8Hk2. You signed in on the Company’s page and approved orders:read orders:write. The Session Yx2b7Q and User ID usr_Q7c1vK are untouched by sign-in. The rule, from section 4.7 of the draft: You may approve fewer scopes than asked, and the Company grants none beyond those asked.

steps.title: The new tag replaces the old
steps.line: pat_3Fz9 replaces pat_8Hk2, which is not sign-out.
steps.caption: The new key has two teeth, one for each scope you approved, and it comes with a new refresh token, pat_3Fz9. The new tag replaces the old one, which the agent revokes. Revoking a replaced token does not sign you out: the account stays signed in through the new one.
steps.picture: No sign-in page is open in your browser. The agent holds a key with two teeth, for orders:read and orders:write, and the refresh token pat_3Fz9. A new sign-in brought a new key and a new refresh token, which replaces the old one; the agent revoked the old one, which is not signing out. The Session Yx2b7Q and User ID usr_Q7c1vK are untouched by sign-in. The rule, from section 4.7 of the draft: Asking again requests every scope still needed, and the new refresh token replaces the old.

steps.title: A copied tag opens nothing
steps.line: invalid_grant: the tag was issued to agent.example.
steps.caption: A refresh token isn’t tied to a Session: any of your Sessions can use the keys it brings. That makes a copy worth stealing, so the Company accepts a refresh token with a client assertion from the agent it was issued to, and refuses it otherwise. A thief can sign only as itself, and gets invalid_grant.

last.reason: the refresh token was issued to https://agent.example/agent.json

after.reason: the refresh token was issued to https://agent.example/agent.json

steps.picture: No sign-in page is open in your browser. The agent holds a key with two teeth, for orders:read and orders:write, and the refresh token pat_3Fz9. A thief sent a copy of the refresh token with its own client assertion and got invalid_grant: the refresh token was issued to https://agent.example/agent.json. The Session Yx2b7Q and User ID usr_Q7c1vK are untouched by sign-in. The rule, from section 4.4 of the draft: A refresh token works only with the agent’s own client assertion.

steps.title: Take the access back, keep your password
steps.line: Now drive it: a refused press says why.
steps.caption: To sign out, the agent revokes every refresh token it holds for your account, and its Session carries on signed out, cart and all. You could instead disconnect the agent in your account settings and keep your account. An agent with your password could only have been blocked. A second account would get its own Session. Press the events to sign in again, approve less or more, or try the trick.

before.reason: the refresh token was issued to https://agent.example/agent.json

steps.picture: No sign-in page is open in your browser. The agent holds no key and no refresh token: it is signed out, and its Session goes on. The agent revoked every refresh token it held for your account. The Session Yx2b7Q and User ID usr_Q7c1vK are untouched by sign-in. The rule, from section 5.5 of the draft: Sign-out revokes every refresh token; the Session continues signed out.

steps.title: The agent shows you a code
steps.line: It checks the link is the Company’s first.
steps.caption: Poppy’s way is OAuth. The agent asks example.com for a sign-in code for the two scopes the exchange needs, orders:read and orders:write, and not addresses. It shows you the code, with a link it has checked is on the Company’s own host, and the Company’s name and domain beside it. Then it polls the Company, five seconds apart, as the Company asked. Until you answer, each poll gets authorization_pending.

The agent has shown you the link and the code WDJB-MJHT, with Example Company and example.com beside them. The agent holds no key and no refresh token. The agent polled the token endpoint with its client assertion and got authorization_pending. The Session Yx2b7Q and User ID usr_Q7c1vK are untouched by sign-in. The rule, from section 4.3 of the draft: Until you answer, each poll gets authorization_pending.

steps.line: scope: orders:read, less than it asked for.

No code passed through your phone to the agent. The response’s scope says orders:read, so the agent knows it got less than it asked for.

The rule, from section 4.3 of the draft: Once you approve, the agent’s next poll returns the tokens.

steps.title: A link to another Company stays hidden
steps.line: Its host is not the Company’s, so you don’t see it.
steps.caption: Device Sign-In is the easier one to phish: whoever holds the device code gets the tokens, and you approve on a page the agent cannot see. Suppose the agent were handed a link to auth.shoes.example. You would approve a sign-in at shoes.example for the Company that asked. So before it shows a link, the agent checks the host. This one is neither auth.example.com nor example.com, nor below either.
